title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping

paper.title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
paper.abstract:
Abstract While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean
Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and
evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that uses input-dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at https://github.com/yandex-research/tabular-regression .

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Despite the growing adoption of deep learning models for tabular data, in practice, it is not entirely clear what objective function should be used to solve regression tasks with DNNs. While the design of advanced regression objectives is an active research direction [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , the traditional Mean Squared Error (MSE) remains widely used. Existing studies evaluate alternative objectives on different datasets, backbones, and tuning protocols, making it difficult to establish which alternatives provide reliable improvements in practice. We revisit traditional and modern regression objectives on 41 established tabular datasets with extensive hyperparameter tuning, focusing on conventional DNNs (pretrained PFNs are outside our scope). We find that most objectives do not consistently improve over a carefully tuned MSE baseline. Two approaches stand out on MLP: Gaussian-smoothed binning objectives [ 1 , 2 ] , which represent targets as distributions over discrete bins, and quantile loss [ 9 ] , which predicts conditional quantiles of p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) via the pinball objective. Of these, quantile loss yields more consistent gains across different backbones. Related evidence comes from the PFN literature: TabICLv2 [ 10 ] adopts quantile loss for regression and reports benefits over MSE and binning; our findings complement this with a systematic comparison in conventional tabular models. Having identified quantile loss as a strong regression objective, we investigate a limitation that remains under standard training: regions with different levels of data uncertainty can reach their best predictive performance at different epochs. Consequently, a single early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions. Such input-dependent variation in target noise is common in tabular data [ 11 ] . We examine this conflict through controlled synthetic experiments and uncertainty-based checkpoint selection on real datasets. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Adaptive Quantile Regression (AdaQR), which incorporates jointly learned, input-dependent smoothing into quantile training. Effectively, by reducing the sensitivity of quantile updates to individual label realizations in high-uncertainty regions, adaptive smoothing aims to delay overfitting there while allowing learning to continue in lower-uncertainty regions. AdaQR is designed as one potential remedy for the mismatch induced by a shared stopping point, which improves upon standard quantile loss on several DNN backbones as we show in our experiments. Our main contributions are: • We benchmark 18 regression objectives on MLP across 41 datasets and evaluate selected objectives on three advanced tabular DNN backbones, using up to 100 hyperparameter tuning trials and the Muon optimizer [ 12 , 13 ] . • We show that most objectives do not consistently beat tuned MSE. Gaussian-smoothed binning objectives and quantile loss stand out on MLPs, while quantile loss provides more consistent gains across the tested backbones. • We identify a limitation of global early stopping in tabular regression: synthetic experiments reveal different preferred stopping epochs across noise levels, while real-data experiments show that selecting checkpoints separately for cohorts defined by estimated uncertainty can improve predictive performance over global selection. • We propose a new AdaQR objective that provides a jointly learned smoothing mechanism for investigating how uncertainty-aware training can mitigate stopping conflicts and evaluate this objective on established tabular backbones.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: Regression objectives. Alternatives to MSE include robust losses [ 14 ] , target discretization [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , conditional distribution modeling [ 15 , 9 , 4 , 16 ] , and representation regularization [ 7 , 8 , 6 ] . We compare representative methods under a common tabular evaluation protocol and describe the individual objectives in the following sections. Early stopping and overfitting. Different parts of a model or subsets of the data can reach their best generalization performance at different training epochs. Heckel and Yilmaz [17] analyze different bias–variance tradeoffs across feature directions and network layers, showing that adjusting learning rates can improve early-stopping performance. Bao et al. [18] observe that some token groups are already overfitting while others remain underfit at the selected checkpoint in sequence-to-sequence models. Berta et al. [19] show that calibration and refinement errors are minimized at different stages of training, including in tabular classification. We extend the uncertainty-based analysis of tabular models [ 11 ] to training trajectories and checkpoint selection, examining how input-dependent noise relates to the epochs at which different regions achieve their best predictive performance. Heteroskedasticity-aware objectives and adaptive smoothing. A large body of work models input-dependent uncertainty in regression [ 20 , 21 ] . However, joint mean and variance estimation can introduce optimization difficulties [ 22 , 23 ] , motivating methods that preserve the mean-prediction accuracy of a corresponding MSE-trained model [ 24 ] . Related work on quantile regression investigates smoothing and local scale adaptation. Tan et al. [25] study convolution smoothing of the pinball loss to improve optimization and statistical estimation. Fasiolo et al. [26] derive covariate-dependent smoothing scales from a preliminary location–scale fit, while Jung et al. [27] estimate local scales using preliminary quantile or absolute-residual regressions. In distributional reinforcement learning, Malekzadeh et al. [28] propose a noise-motivated generalization of quantile-Huber loss with adaptive parameter adjustment. AdaQR combines an energy-distance objective with an input-dependent smoothing head learned jointly with the neural quantile predictor. We investigate this formulation through its effects on uncertainty-dependent training dynamics and tabular point prediction.

sections.heading: 3. Revisiting regression objectives
sections.text: Notation. We consider supervised regression on tabular data. Let D = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 n D=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} denote a dataset, where x i ∈ ℝ d x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the feature vector and y i ∈ ℝ y_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is the target. We denote the neural model by f θ : ℝ d → ℝ d ′ f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}} , where the output dimension d ′ d^{\prime} depends on the objective and need not equal one. For pointwise objectives, the loss on an observation is l ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( x i ) , y i ) l(f_{\theta}(x_{i}),y_{i}) .

sections.heading: 3.1 Losses
sections.text: Figure 1: Performance comparison of different objective functions using an MLP backbone across 41 BeyondArena datasets. ( Left ) Average rank performance across all datasets. ( Right ) Relative RMSE improvement over the standard MSE baseline, visualizing the magnitude of performance gains or degradation. The box plots visualize the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of the jitter plots. Notation details are provided in the beginning of Section . We compare the following regression objectives. Traditional losses. MSE penalizes squared errors, MAE penalizes absolute errors, and Huber loss [ 29 ] combines quadratic penalties for small errors with linear penalties for large ones. Binning-based losses. These methods discretize the target range into bins and train a categorical prediction head to match a target distribution. Hard Binning assigns each target to its nearest bin, while Soft Binning distributes probability mass according to Gaussian weights evaluated at bin centers [ 2 ] . HL-Gaussian instead integrates a truncated Gaussian density over each bin [ 1 ] . Joint end-to-end encoding learns the target distribution using an auxiliary encoder and a reconstruction objective [ 2 ] . All four methods return the predicted expectation over bin centers. Softmax-MSE uses the same prediction head but directly minimizes the squared error of this expectation [ 2 ] . Quantile regression. The model predicts a grid of conditional quantiles using the pinball loss [ 9 ] ; their average serves as the scalar prediction. Likelihood-based objectives. Gaussian NLL jointly learns a conditional mean and variance. β \beta -NLL reweights this objective by a detached power of the predicted variance to address optimization difficulties [ 22 ] . Mixture Density Networks model the conditional distribution as a Gaussian mixture [ 15 ] . The autoregressive approach of Song and Bahri [4] instead predicts tokenized targets using next-token cross-entropy. We evaluate both its normalized and unnormalized target encodings. Additional objectives and regularizers. GAR combines pointwise and pairwise terms to capture target values and their differences [ 5 ] . Ordinal Entropy [ 6 ] and ROT-REG [ 8 ] augment regression training with representation regularization, using entropy-based and optimal-transport-based terms, respectively. We provide a detailed description of all objectives in Appendix .

sections.heading: 3.2 Experiments
sections.text: Datasets. We evaluate a subset of 41 regression datasets from BeyondArena [ 30 ] , excluding three computationally demanding datasets to keep hyperparameter tuning feasible within our 24-hour budget. We use the first predefined split of each retained dataset. Further details are provided in Appendix .

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Implementation details
sections.text: Model backbone. We first compare regression objectives on the simplest MLP backbone, then evaluate selected objectives on additional advanced architectures. Depending on the objective, the prediction head outputs either a scalar, y ^ i = f θ ​ ( x i ) ∈ ℝ \hat{y}_{i}=f_{\theta}(x_{i})\in\mathbb{R} , or a vector parameterizing the corresponding predictive output. Experimental setup. We follow the evaluation protocol of Gorishniy et al. [31] , detailed in Appendix . Unless stated otherwise, we use Muon-based training [ 12 ] , following recent evidence of its effectiveness on tabular data [ 13 ] . For each dataset and objective, we tune the model, objective, and optimizer hyperparameters on the validation set. We then retrain the selected configuration from scratch across 15 random seeds and report test RMSE. Method comparisons use the mean and standard deviation across these seeds, as described in Appendix .

sections.heading: 3.2.3 Advanced backbones
sections.text: Having identified promising objectives on MLP, we examine whether their benefits transfer to other state-of-the-art backbone architectures. We retain HL-Gaussian as a representative binning-based objective and compare it and quantile loss against MSE. Following the same evaluation protocol, we train TabPack with periodic feature embeddings [ 33 ] , TabM-mini with PLE-Q embeddings [ 31 ] , and RealMLP [ 34 ] . Implementation details are provided in Appendix . Table shows that quantile loss provides more consistent gains across the tested backbones than HL-Gaussian. In contrast, quantile loss achieves positive median improvements and more wins than losses on every tested backbone. sections.heading: 4. Quantile regression under heteroskedasticity
sections.text: The benchmark in Section identifies several regression objectives that consistently outperform the MSE baseline. While HL-Gaussian and quantile regression (QR) perform comparably on a plain MLP, QR is more robust across backbones (Table ). Therefore, we focus on QR for the remainder of our analysis. QR predicts conditional quantiles without assuming a parametric family for p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) , allowing the predicted distribution’s shape and scale to vary across inputs. This flexibility is particularly beneficial for tabular data, where the conditional variance Var ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] \mathrm{Var}[y\mid x] , often termed data uncertainty , changes substantially with x x (i.e., the data is heteroskedastic ). Kartashev et al. [11] identify regions of low and high data uncertainty in several established tabular datasets, and demonstrate that dataset-wise aggregate scores often obscure how methods perform across these different regions. However, modeling input-dependent distributions does not guarantee that regions with different noise levels achieve their optimal predictive performance at the same epoch. Standard global early stopping selects a single checkpoint based on average validation error, applying it uniformly to all inputs. We first examine how prediction errors evolve during training across different uncertainty levels (Section ). We then test whether selecting checkpoints separately for different uncertainty cohorts improves upon doing so for random cohorts of the same size (Section ). Together, these experiments reveal an optimization challenge that distributional flexibility alone cannot resolve, motivating the adaptive objective introduced in Section . Both experiments in this section require a per-point estimate of data uncertainty and are most interpretable when this estimate is exact and test targets are noise-free. To demonstrate the claims of this section in a controlled environment that has these traits, we construct a synthetic dataset y = f ⁡ ( x ) + ε y=f(x)+\varepsilon , with noise added only to training targets, so test RMSE directly measures recovery of f = 𝔼 ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] f=\mathbb{E}[y\mid x] . We use two variants sharing exactly the same f f and x x : heteroskedastic , with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ ​ ( x ) 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma(x)^{2}) , and homoskedastic , with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) , serving as a control. Importantly, for this dataset, levels of true data uncertainty σ 2 \sigma^{2} are known to us exactly. See Appendix for details. To estimate uncertainty on real data we use a CatBoost model [ 35 ] trained via Gaussian negative log-likelihood on the real datasets, utilizing the predicted σ ⁡ ( x ) \sigma(x) as our uncertainty estimate. To prevent data leakage, this estimator is fit exclusively on the training split and applied to validation and test points during inference.

sections.heading: 4.1 Optimal stopping epochs vary by uncertainty region
sections.text: In this subsection we investigate whether models require different stopping epochs for regions with varying data uncertainty. This requires analyzing the test error disaggregated by uncertainty level across epochs. The uncertainty plot [ 11 ] provides this perspective. Figure (a) shows an MLP trained with the quantile loss on the heteroskedastic synthetic dataset. Each curve corresponds to one epoch and displays the point-wise change in squared error relative to a reference epoch (the one with the best aggregate validation MSE), plotted against data uncertainty. Before the reference epoch, the model performs better on high-uncertainty points and worse on low-uncertainty ones; afterward, this trend reverses. In other words, the model starts overfitting high-uncertainty regions before it finishes fitting low-uncertainty ones, and the reference epoch is merely a compromise between these competing dynamics. To verify that this pattern stems from varying noise levels rather than intrinsic properties of x x or f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , Figure (c) repeats the experiment on the homoskedastic variant (same f f , constant noise scale, with samples sorted as in the heteroskedastic version). The effect disappears: performance changes across the displayed epochs are largely unrelated to the uncertainty ordering inherited from the heteroskedastic variant. Ideally, a model would retain its early-epoch error on high-uncertainty points while achieving its late-epoch error on low-uncertainty points, improving upon the QR baseline. However, Figure (a) only illustrates this misalignment on synthetic data and does not quantify the resulting performance loss. Section closes both gaps. Figure 2: In this synthetic experiment, heteroskedastic noise creates a mismatch between the stopping epochs preferred by low- and high-uncertainty regions, while AdaQR mitigates this effect. Uncertainty plots [ 11 ] for an MLP trained with (a) quantile loss and (b) AdaQR on the heteroskedastic dataset, and (c) quantile loss on the homoskedastic counterpart. Each curve shows the smoothed point-wise difference in squared test error relative to the reference epoch with the best aggregate validation MSE; negative values indicate improvement. Test samples are ordered by increasing uncertainty in the heteroskedastic dataset, with the same ordering used in all panels. Under heteroskedastic noise, earlier epochs perform relatively better on high-uncertainty points and later epochs on low-uncertainty points, indicating that different uncertainty regions favor different stopping times. This separation is reduced with AdaQR and disappears when the noise is homoskedastic.

sections.heading: 4.2 Measuring the impact of epoch misalignment
sections.text: To quantify the performance penalty implied by the epoch misalignment in Figure (a), we evaluate a hypothetical strategy of per-cohort early stopping . This approach requires dividing the validation and test sets into groups of comparable data uncertainty, termed cohorts . To construct these, we compute the K − 1 K-1 empirical k K \tfrac{k}{K} -quantiles of the estimated uncertainty σ ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{\sigma}(x) on the validation set. These thresholds are used to split both the validation and test sets into K K cohorts, ordered from lowest (cohort 1 1 ) to highest (cohort K K ) uncertainty. Deriving these thresholds strictly from the validation set prevents data leakage, yielding equal-sized validation cohorts and test cohorts that are balanced up to sampling noise. With the cohorts established, we save a model checkpoint at every epoch during training. For each uncertainty cohort k k , we select the checkpoint e k ∗ e_{k}^{*} that minimizes the validation MSE restricted specifically to that group. During inference, each test point is routed to the checkpoint e k ∗ e_{k}^{*} corresponding to its uncertainty cohort. Because this approach assigns exactly one checkpoint to each test example, the resulting aggregated test RMSE reflects the empirical benefit of tailoring stopping times to local uncertainty levels. To accurately isolate this benefit, we cannot simply compare the resulting RMSE to standard global early stopping. While per-cohort selection allows the model to choose K K different epochs, each choice relies on only a fraction ( 1 / K 1/K ) of the validation data. To create a fair baseline, we apply the exact same procedure to random cohorts of matching size, created by randomly permuting the points before splitting. These random groups suffer the same penalty of smaller validation sets but contain no uncertainty information. Therefore, comparing uncertainty cohorts directly to random cohorts isolates the advantage of grouping by local noise levels. Table presents the relative improvements in test RMSE when using uncertainty-based (U) and random (R) cohorts compared to standard global (G) early stopping. To minimize the negative effects of smaller validation sets, we restrict this experiment to the seven largest datasets from our benchmark, reporting results for K = 5 K=5 and K = 10 K=10 . The results demonstrate that uncertainty-based selection improves median RMSE over global selection by 0.18% and 0.114% for five and ten cohorts, respectively. Under our comparison rule, both configurations record three wins, four ties, and no losses across the seven datasets. Furthermore, the drop in overall performance when increasing from K = 5 K=5 to K = 10 K=10 cohorts is consistent with increased checkpoint-selection noise from smaller validation subsets. The table also includes the homoskedastic variant of our synthetic dataset, which shares the same features x x and noiseless target function f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , but features a constant noise scale σ \sigma . This allows us to apply the exact same cohort splits used for the heteroskedastic variant. If σ ⁡ ( x ) \sigma(x) were merely acting as a proxy for partitioning the feature space into regions of similar inputs, both variants would show similar gains. Instead, performance on the homoskedastic version worsens when applying uncertainty-based splits, while the opposite is true for the heteroskedastic variant. Thus, the benefit stems specifically from adapting to how varying label noise alters training dynamics, not from the spatial structure of the inputs. Per-cohort early stopping, however, is not a practical solution: it requires storing numerous checkpoints and assigning test points to cohorts during inference. These results motivate adapting the objective to delay overfitting in high-uncertainty regions while allowing learning to continue in low-uncertainty regions. sections.heading: 5. Adaptive quantile regression
sections.text: To address the stopping-time mismatch identified in Section , we introduce AdaQR, a quantile objective with jointly learned, input-dependent smoothing inspired by Adaptive Label Smoothing [ 36 ] . By applying stronger smoothing in high-uncertainty regions, we aim to postpone overfitting there. Up to quantile discretization, quantile loss is proportional to the squared Energy Distance between the predicted distribution and a Dirac δ \delta distribution at the observed target y y . Appendix details this connection through the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). To incorporate adaptive smoothing, we replace this point mass with a Gaussian distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( y , σ l 2 ) \mathcal{N}(y,\sigma_{l}^{2}) centered around the target, where σ l 2 \sigma_{l}^{2} is a learned variance predicted from the input x x . We design our loss function such that a larger conditional variance Var ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] \mathrm{Var}[y\mid x] yields a larger predicted σ l 2 \sigma_{l}^{2} . Specifically, the loss function we use is ℒ ⁡ ( F , y , σ l ) = 1 2 ​ 𝒟 2 ​ ( F , 𝒩 ⁡ ( y , σ l 2 ) ) + λ ​ σ l , \mathcal{L}(F,y,\sigma_{l})=\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{D}^{2}\bigl(F,\mathcal{N}(y,\sigma_{l}^{2})\bigr)+\lambda\sigma_{l}, where 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denotes the Energy Distance [ 37 ] . The first term is half of the squared Energy Distance, where the predicted distribution F F is estimated through the predicted quantiles q i q_{i} . sections.heading: 5.1 AdaQR results
sections.text: We first evaluate AdaQR’s predictive accuracy. In the following sections, we analyze the role of adaptive smoothing, the quality of the learned uncertainty estimates, and AdaQR’s effect on the global stopping compromise. Our main comparison covers 28 datasets with at least 1,000 training samples, excluding the Tiny category of BeyondArena [ 30 ] . Since AdaQR trains an additional σ l \sigma_{l} logit jointly with the main predictions and requires tuning λ \lambda , which can complicate optimization on very small datasets, we exclude such datasets from the main comparison. We follow our standard evaluation protocol with Muon-based training on MLP, TabPack [ 33 ] , RealMLP [ 34 ] , and TabM-mini with PLE-Q embeddings [ 31 ] . On MLP, we additionally evaluate Gaussian NLL and β \beta -NLL as heteroskedastic baselines. For RealMLP, we use a scale-regularized variant, denoted by AdaQR † , motivated by the uncertainty-estimation analysis and described in Appendix . Table shows that AdaQR achieves positive median RMSE improvements over MSE on all four backbones. Its median gains over MSE are also larger than those of quantile loss, with the clearest differences on TabM and RealMLP and a small difference on TabPack. These results support AdaQR as a useful training alternative, while showing that its benefits vary across backbones.

sections.heading: 5.4 Effect on the Global Stopping Compromise
sections.text: The synthetic results in Figure suggest that AdaQR alleviates the mismatch between optimal stopping epochs across uncertainty regions. sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we systematically revisit regression objectives for tabular deep learning, comparing 18 objectives on 41 datasets and evaluating leading approaches across multiple backbones. Quantile loss emerges as a consistently strong alternative to carefully tuned MSE. Yet a strong objective does not eliminate the limitations of global early stopping: regions with different noise levels can peak at different training epochs, making a shared checkpoint a compromise. Motivated by this, we introduce AdaQR, which uses jointly learned, input-dependent smoothing as one possible remedy and improves predictions in several settings, with benefits varying across backbones and datasets. Our findings highlight that progress in tabular regression requires attention not only to what models optimize, but also to how different parts of the data are learned over time.

sections.heading: 7. Limitations
sections.text: Our study identifies uncertainty-dependent stopping conflicts as an opportunity to improve tabular regression, but our understanding of the underlying training dynamics remains incomplete. AdaQR helps mitigate these stopping conflicts: on real datasets, cohort-based checkpoint selection yields smaller improvements for AdaQR than for standard quantile regression (Section ), yet still provides additional gains. This residual benefit suggests that adaptive smoothing does not fully resolve differences in preferred stopping times across uncertainty regions. Further work is needed to understand when these conflicts arise and to explore alternative objectives, training procedures, or checkpoint-selection strategies that can address them more effectively. AdaQR’s predictive gains also vary in magnitude across backbones, and its main evaluation excludes Tiny datasets, although results including them are reported in Appendix .

sections.heading: Appendix A Datasets
sections.text: Our benchmark comprises 41 datasets from BeyondArena [ 30 ] . We exclude maps_router_eta_1m , delivery_eta_1m and cooking_time_1m from the evaluation due to their combination of high numerical dimensionality (992 for maps_router_eta_1m ), high categorical cardinality (135131 for cooking_time_1m ) and large sample size (1.25 million for all three of them). Under our chosen preprocessing and training pipeline, these characteristics make exhaustive hyperparameter tuning infeasible within the 24-hour computational budget imposed for each dataset. We use the lite subset of the benchmark (i.e., the first split of each dataset). Importantly, GAR[MSE], GAR[MAE] and Ordinal Entropy on MLP show abnormal behavior and fail to converge on airfoil_self_noise and on telemonitoring_parkinsons_biomedical_voice_measurements . To retain these datasets in the aggregate comparisons, we replace each failed result with the worst result among the methods that converged on the same dataset using the MLP backbone.

sections.heading: B.1 Experimental protocol
sections.text: Data preprocessing. For each dataset, the same preprocessing is used. First, we treat binary features as categorical. Both binary and categorical features are then transformed using ordinal encoding. By default, numerical features are processed via a slightly modified version of quantile normalization from Scikit-learn [ 38 ] (see the code). Finally, targets are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, though all final metrics are computed on the original scale. The only exception is the evaluation of decoders [ 4 ] , where we follow the authors’ protocol by either mapping targets to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] (for the normalized decoder) or applying no transformations (for the unnormalized version). Training Process . We use Muon [ 12 ] to optimize all layer weight matrices, while AdamW [ 32 ] is used for bias parameters and the output-layer weight matrix. We do not apply learning rate schedulers. We apply global gradient clipping to 1.0. For each dataset, we use the predefined batch size (see Appendix ) and continue training until there are patience consecutive epochs without improvements on the validation set; we set patience = 16 \texttt{patience}=16 . Hyperparameter tuning. For each experiment, we carefully tune optimizer, objective and backbone hyperparameters using Optuna’s TPE sampler [ 39 ] , for 100 trials with 24-hour tune time limitation. We use RMSE computed on the validation split as the optimization objective. We provide full parameter spaces in Appendix . Evaluation. After the best hyperparameters are found, we run the model with those parameters on 15 different random seeds and report the performance on the test part of the dataset. For each dataset, we use mean and standard deviation of test metrics (RMSE) over these random seeds to compare methods as described in Appendix .

sections.heading: B.2 Ranks and metrics
sections.text: As we focus exclusively on regression tasks, we report Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) as a primary metric. As mentioned in Appendix , all models and objectives are evaluated on 15 random seeds. We compare methods using two aggregation approaches. Relative Improvement. For each dataset, we compute the mean RMSE over 15 seeds and calculate its relative improvement (in %) over the baseline (typically the standard MSE objective). These values are shown in the right panel of Figure . Meanwhile, in the “Improv. (%)” columns of tables, we further aggregate them and report their median over the benchmark datasets. Ranks. For each dataset, we assign ranks based on a conservative order relation. Method A A (with mean RMSE A μ A_{\mu} and standard deviation A σ A_{\sigma} ) is considered significantly better than method B B if A μ + A σ < B μ A_{\mu}+A_{\sigma}<B_{\mu} (We use this approach for finding W/T/L with A A being the reference method). Intuitively, this approach groups methods into “tiers,” ensuring that negligible gains are not counted as wins on individual datasets. Specifically, ranks are computed independently for each dataset using a top-down procedure. We first sort the methods in ascending order of their mean RMSE. The best model is assigned rank 1 and serves as the initial reference. We then iterate through the remaining models: all methods that are not significantly worse than the current reference (according to the aforementioned rule) also receive rank 1. The first model that fails this criterion is assigned rank 2 and becomes the new reference for subsequent comparisons. This process continues until all models are ranked. The left panel of Figure illustrates the mean and standard deviation of these ranks across the benchmark.

sections.heading: B.3 Support construction for distributional losses
sections.text: For every binning-based distributional objective we construct the support [ a , b ] [a,b] as follows: (i) we compute the range between the 0.005- and 0.995-quantiles of the training labels distribution (we employ quantiles rather than min-max values to mitigate the impact of outliers while capturing the effective support of the distribution); (ii) we expand this range by adding the same interval on both the left and right sides; (iii) we then uniformly partition it into bins. The uniform binning is the most common in distributional regression research [ 1 , 2 ] and performs stably in our experiments.

sections.heading: Appendix C Detailed description of regression objectives
sections.text: Notation. We consider supervised regression tasks on tabular data. Let D = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 n D=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} denote the dataset, where x i ∈ ℝ d x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the feature vector and y i ∈ ℝ y_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is the label for the i i -th datapoint. We denote the deep learning model by f θ : ℝ d → ℝ d ′ f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}} , where d ′ d^{\prime} is the output dimension, which is not necessarily equal to 1. Let l ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) l(\cdot,\cdot) be the loss function. The loss on a given sample is then defined as l = l ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( x ) , y ) l=l(f_{\theta}(x),y) .

sections.heading: C.1.1 Traditional losses
sections.text: The first group of objectives in our comparison includes canonical regression losses. Here, any values denoted by a hat ⋅ ^ \hat{\cdot} correspond to predictions produced by our model. • MSE (Mean Squared Error, or l 2 l_{2} loss) is the standard objective for most regression tasks: l = l 2 ​ ( y ^ , y ) = ( y ^ − y ) 2 l=l_{2}(\hat{y},y)=(\hat{y}-y)^{2} • MAE (Mean Absolute Error, or l 1 l_{1} loss) provides robustness against outliers by penalizing errors linearly: l = l 1 ​ ( y ^ , y ) = | y ^ − y | l=l_{1}(\hat{y},y)=|\hat{y}-y| • Huber loss [ 29 ] is a middle ground between MSE and MAE: l = l δ ​ ( y ^ , y ) = { 1 2 ​ ( y − y ^ ) 2 , if ​ | y ^ − y | ≤ δ δ ⋅ | y − y ^ | − 1 2 ​ δ 2 , if ​ | y ^ − y | > δ l=l_{\delta}(\hat{y},y)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}(y-\hat{y})^{2},&\text{if }|\hat{y}-y|\leq\delta\\ \delta\cdot|y-\hat{y}|-\frac{1}{2}\delta^{2},&\text{if }|\hat{y}-y|>\delta\end{cases}

sections.heading: C.1.2 Binning-based losses
sections.text: Among various regression objectives, the binning-based losses [ 41 , 1 , 2 ] stand out as a promising option for regression tasks and are reported to be beneficial across diverse domains [ 3 ] . The core idea is to discretize scalar targets using a grid of consecutive bins. Formally, consider a sample ( x , y ) ∈ D (x,y)\in D . The regression label y y is mapped to a probability vector 𝐩 = ( p 1 , … , p d ′ ) \mathbf{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{d^{\prime}}) over the d ′ d^{\prime} bins on the support [ a , b ] [a,b] . Here, the i i -th bin is the interval [ l i , r i ] [l_{i},r_{i}] with center c i c_{i} . Given the model’s logits f θ ​ ( x ) f_{\theta}(x) , let 𝐪 = softmax ​ ( f θ ​ ( x ) ) \mathbf{q}=\text{softmax}(f_{\theta}(x)) . The model is trained to approximate the target distribution 𝐩 \mathbf{p} via the KL divergence: l = l KL ( f θ ( x ) , y ) = D KL ( 𝐩 ∥ 𝐪 ) . l=l_{\textsc{KL}}(f_{\theta}(x),y)=D_{\textsc{KL}}(\mathbf{p}\,\|\,\mathbf{q}). At inference, model predictions are computed by taking the expectation over the bins: y ^ = ∑ i 𝐪 i ⋅ c i . \hat{y}=\sum_{i}\mathbf{q}_{i}\cdot c_{i}. The particular form of the target distribution is typically the same for all datapoints and using different forms of the target distributions results in different regression objectives. Below, we describe several binning-based objectives that we include in the comparison. Hard Binning [ 41 , 2 ] maps each y y to a one-hot vector 𝐩 \mathbf{p} by assigning it to the nearest bin center. Soft Binning [ 2 ] improves Hard Binning by performing soft mapping to the dense probability vector: 𝐩 = softmax ⁡ ( − | c 1 − y | 2 2 ​ σ 2 , … , − | c d ′ − y | 2 2 ​ σ 2 ) , \mathbf{p}=\mathrm{softmax}\left(-\frac{|c_{1}-y|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}},\dots,-\frac{|c_{d^{\prime}}-y|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right), where σ \sigma is a global (shared across the dataset) hyperparameter controlling the spread of probability mass over the bins. HL-Gaussian [ 1 ] constructs 𝐩 \mathbf{p} by discretizing the truncated Gaussian distribution with mean y y and fixed variance σ 2 \sigma^{2} over [ a , b ] [a,b] . Specifically, given the density ρ ⁡ ( t ∣ y ) = 1 Z ​ 2 ​ π ​ σ 2 ​ e − ( t − y ) 2 2 ​ σ 2 \rho(t\mid y)=\frac{1}{Z\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}e^{-\frac{(t-y)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}} the bin probabilities are 𝐩 i = 1 Z ​ ( Φ ⁡ ( r i − y σ ) − Φ ⁡ ( l i − y σ ) ) \mathbf{p}_{i}=\frac{1}{Z}\left(\Phi\left(\frac{r_{i}-y}{\sigma}\right)-\Phi\left(\frac{l_{i}-y}{\sigma}\right)\right) where Φ \Phi is the cdf-function for 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathcal{N}(0,1) and Z Z is the normalization constant. This is achieved by adding a reconstruction term (recovering y y from 𝐩 \mathbf{p} ) to the D KL ( 𝐩 ∥ 𝐪 ) D_{\textsc{KL}}(\mathbf{p}\,\|\,\mathbf{q}) loss.

sections.heading: C.1.3 Quantile loss
sections.text: Quantile loss [ 9 ] offers an alternative approach to modeling conditional distributions p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) by directly predicting specific quantiles of the target variable. Specifically, for a given input x x , the model predicts N N quantiles y ^ τ 1 , y ^ τ 2 , … , y ^ τ N \hat{y}_{\tau_{1}},\hat{y}_{\tau_{2}},\dots,\hat{y}_{\tau_{N}} corresponding to quantile levels τ 1 , τ 2 , … , τ N ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \tau_{1},\tau_{2},\dots,\tau_{N}\in(0,1) . Each quantile prediction y ^ τ i \hat{y}_{\tau_{i}} is trained using the pinball loss function: ρ τ i ​ ( y , y ^ τ i ) = { τ i ​ ( y − y ^ τ i ) , if ​ y ≥ y ^ τ i ( 1 − τ i ) ​ ( y ^ τ i − y ) , if ​ y < y ^ τ i \rho_{\tau_{i}}(y,\hat{y}_{\tau_{i}})=\begin{cases}\tau_{i}(y-\hat{y}_{\tau_{i}}),&\text{if }y\geq\hat{y}_{\tau_{i}}\\ (1-\tau_{i})(\hat{y}_{\tau_{i}}-y),&\text{if }y<\hat{y}_{\tau_{i}}\end{cases} where τ i ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \tau_{i}\in(0,1) represents the target quantile level. The overall loss function is then computed as the average pinball loss across all N N quantiles: l = l QR ​ ( f θ ​ ( x ) , y ) = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ρ τ i ​ ( y , f θ , i ​ ( x ) ) l=l_{\textsc{QR}}(f_{\theta}(x),y)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\rho_{\tau_{i}}(y,f_{\theta,i}(x)) where f θ , i ​ ( x ) f_{\theta,i}(x) denotes the model’s prediction for the i i -th quantile. During inference, the final prediction y ^ \hat{y} is typically obtained by taking the average of all predicted quantiles: y ^ = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N y ^ τ i . \hat{y}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{y}_{\tau_{i}}. This approach provides a more direct characterization of the conditional distribution compared to binning methods, while avoiding the discretization of the output space.

sections.heading: C.1.4 Modeling full conditional distributions in the arbitrary form
sections.text: An alternative paradigm to solve a regression problem has been employed in several recent works [ 16 , 4 ] that model the conditional distributions p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y|x) without any assumptions about their parametric form. In our experimental comparison, we include the most recent approach proposed by Song and Bahri [4] that relies on the autoregressive decoder. Specifically, the approach uses a small autoregressive decoding head on top of an MLP backbone. Both MLP and decoder are trained jointly for the next-token (where tokens represent digits) prediction with a cross-entropy loss. The decoder predicts the sequence of tokens t 1 , … , t k t_{1},\dots,t_{k} that represent the target y y in an autoregressive manner. Formally, let ϕ ⁡ ( x ) \phi(x) be the representation produced by the MLP encoder. The model estimates the conditional distribution p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) via the following factorization: p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) = ∏ i = 1 k p ⁡ ( t i ∣ t 1 , … , t i − 1 , ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ) . p(y\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}p(t_{i}\mid t_{1},\dots,t_{i-1},\phi(x)). In our study, we evaluate two versions of this decoder described by the method’s authors. In the normalized variant, targets are mapped to the [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] interval using min-max transformation before tokenization. In the unnormalized variant, targets are represented as floating-point numbers in a base- B B system: y = ± B e ⋅ m y=\pm B^{e}\cdot m , where the exponent e e and mantissa m ∈ [ 1 , B ) m\in[1,B) are predicted.

sections.heading: C.1.5 Other losses
sections.text: In this section we list several additional regression objectives that are included in our evaluation. • GAR (Gradient aligned regression) [ 5 ] combines point-wise and pair-wise terms to better match the gradient and magnitude of the target function. • Softmax-MSE [ 2 ] uses a softmax binning head followed by computing the expectation and MSE loss: l = ( ∑ i 𝐪 i ⋅ c i − y ) 2 l=\left(\textstyle\sum_{i}\mathbf{q}_{i}\cdot c_{i}-y\right)^{2} where c i c_{i} and 𝐪 \mathbf{q} follow the binning losses notation from Section . • Ordinal Entropy loss [ 6 ] is an objective that enables NNs to learn better feature representations Z Z (specifically, to maximize mutual information ℐ ⁡ ( Z , Y ) = ℋ ⁡ ( Z ) − ℋ ⁡ ( Z ∣ Y ) \mathcal{I}(Z,Y)=\mathcal{H}(Z)-\mathcal{H}(Z\mid Y) ), by adding two additional terms to the initial regression loss. • ROT-REG [ 8 ] is an optimal transport based regularizer that similarly allows the model to enhance learned representations by tightening them. • NLL assumes p ⁡ ( y | x ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ ⁡ ( x ) , σ 2 ​ ( x ) ) p(y|x)=\mathcal{N}(\mu(x),\sigma^{2}(x)) and minimizes the negative log-likelihood: l = 1 2 ​ log ⁡ σ ^ 2 + ( μ ^ − y ) 2 2 ​ σ ^ 2 . l=\frac{1}{2}\log\hat{\sigma}^{2}+\frac{(\hat{\mu}-y)^{2}}{2\hat{\sigma}^{2}}. • β \beta -NLL [ 22 ] extends NLL by reweighting each sample by ⌊ σ ^ 2 ​ β ⌋ \lfloor\hat{\sigma}^{2\beta}\rfloor to improve optimization stability, where ⌊ ⋅ ⌋ \lfloor\cdot\rfloor denotes the stop-gradient operation. • Mixture Density Networks [ 15 ] model the conditional distribution p ⁡ ( y | x ) p(y|x) as a Gaussian mixture.

sections.heading: Appendix D Detailed description of the dataset used in Section
sections.text: To evaluate the robustness of our method under strictly controlled noise conditions, we construct both homoskedastic and heteroskedastic synthetic datasets. Below are the details regarding the process of generation. Dataset Size and Splits: The total dataset size is N = 50,000 N=50,000 . We split this into 20,000 training examples, 15,000 validation examples, and 15,000 test examples. Importantly, while the training targets contain injected noise, the validation and test targets are completely noise-free ( y clean y_{\text{clean}} ). This allows us to accurately evaluate how well the models uncover the true underlying conditional expectation. Base Network Architecture: We use a standardized Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) generator to create non-linear mappings. To ensure stable scales across different initializations, the outputs of this generator are explicitly standardized to have zero mean and unit variance using statistics calculated over an initial batch of 10,000 10,000 Gaussian noise samples. All MLPs use hidden dimensions of 256 and ReLU activations. Feature Generation ( X X ): 1. We sample a 40-dimensional latent from the standard multivariate Gaussian distribution: z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I 40 ) z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{40}) . 2. We map z z through a 3-layer MLP generator to produce a 100-dimensional informative feature vector x real ∈ ℝ 100 x_{\text{real}}\in\mathbb{R}^{100} . We use this step to imitate the complex relationships between features that are often found in tabular data. 3. To introduce irrelevant features, we sample 16-dimensional standard Gaussian noise x noisy ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I 16 ) x_{\text{noisy}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{16}) . 4. The final feature vector is the concatenation of the informative and noisy features: x = [ x real , x noisy ] ∈ ℝ 116 x=[x_{\text{real}},x_{\text{noisy}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{116} . Target Generation ( Y Y ): The clean target values, f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , are generated by passing the informative features x real x_{\text{real}} through a 2-layer MLP f θ f_{\theta} . To create the noisy training targets y noisy y_{\text{noisy}} , we inject Gaussian noise ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) according to one of two settings: • Homoskedastic Dataset: The variance is constant across the entire input space. y noisy = y clean + σ ​ ϵ , where ​ σ = 4.0 y_{\text{noisy}}=y_{\text{clean}}+\sigma\epsilon,\quad\text{where }\sigma=4.0 • Heteroskedastic Dataset: The standard deviation σ ⁡ ( x ) \sigma(x) depends non-linearly on the informative features. We pass x real x_{\text{real}} through another 2-layer MLP g ϕ g_{\phi} to obtain a scalar. This scalar is pushed through a Standard Normal Cumulative Distribution Function Φ \Phi to bound it in ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) . We then scale, shift, and exponentiate it to create a smooth, variable standard deviation profile: σ ⁡ ( x ) = exp ⁡ ( Φ ⁡ ( g ϕ ​ ( x real ) ) × 4.5 − 2.0 ) \sigma(x)=\exp\Big(\Phi(g_{\phi}(x_{\text{real}}))\times 4.5-2.0\ \Big) y noisy = y clean + σ ⁡ ( x ) ​ ϵ y_{\text{noisy}}=y_{\text{clean}}+\sigma(x)\epsilon To ensure exact reproducibility, the process uses manual random seeds before any generation.

sections.heading: Appendix E Quantile loss and Energy Distance
sections.text: There exists a well-known relation between the quantile loss and the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) [ 42 , 43 ] : CRPS ⁡ ( F , y ) \displaystyle\mathrm{CRPS}(F,y) = ∫ − ∞ + ∞ ( F ( z ) − 𝟙 { z ≥ y } ) 2 d z \displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\bigl(F(z)-\mathbbm{1}\{z\geq y\}\bigr)^{2}\,dz = 2 ​ ∫ 0 1 ρ τ ​ ( y , Q F ​ ( τ ) ) ​ d τ ≈ 2 ⋅ l QR ​ ( Q F ​ ( ⋅ ) , y ) , \displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{1}\rho_{\tau}(y,Q_{F}(\tau))\,d\tau\approx 2\cdot l_{\mathrm{QR}}(Q_{F}(\cdot),y), where F F is a CDF, Q F Q_{F} is its quantile function, and ρ τ \rho_{\tau} is the pinball loss (Section ). The approximation replaces the integral over quantile levels with an average over the finite uniform grid used by our models. Thus, up to this discretization and a constant factor, minimizing the quantile loss is equivalent to minimizing CRPS. For real-valued random variables with finite first moments, the squared Energy Distance is [ 37 ] 𝒟 2 ​ ( F , G ) = 2 ​ 𝔼 ​ | X − Y | − 𝔼 ​ | X − X ′ | − 𝔼 ​ | Y − Y ′ | , \mathcal{D}^{2}(F,G)=2\mathbb{E}|X-Y|-\mathbb{E}|X-X^{\prime}|-\mathbb{E}|Y-Y^{\prime}|, where X , X ′ ∼ F X,X^{\prime}\sim F and Y , Y ′ ∼ G Y,Y^{\prime}\sim G are mutually independent. When G = δ y G=\delta_{y} , the Dirac distribution concentrated at y y , this gives CRPS ⁡ ( F , y ) = 𝔼 ​ | X − y | − 1 2 ​ 𝔼 ​ | X − X ′ | = 1 2 ​ 𝒟 2 ​ ( F , δ y ) . \mathrm{CRPS}(F,y)=\mathbb{E}|X-y|-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}|X-X^{\prime}|=\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{D}^{2}(F,\delta_{y}). This identity provides the Energy Distance interpretation of quantile loss used in Section : the predicted distribution is compared with a point mass at the observed target. AdaQR replaces this point mass with an input-dependent Gaussian smoothing distribution.

sections.heading: Appendix G Scale regularization for RealMLP
sections.text: For RealMLP, we augment AdaQR with an auxiliary scale regularizer, denoting the resulting objective by AdaQR † . Below, we describe its motivation, formulation, and effect on uncertainty estimation.

sections.heading: G.1 Uncertainty estimation in RealMLP
sections.text: Proposition characterizes the population optimum under Gaussian assumptions. In practice, however, there is no guarantee that training reaches this optimum. In particular, a model can correctly rank inputs by uncertainty while producing inaccurate absolute scales. We compare TabM and RealMLP on our heteroskedastic synthetic dataset, where the true data uncertainty is known, converting smoothing scales into noise-scale estimates via ( ). TabM already recovers the underlying data uncertainty reasonably well and consistently across ensemble members (Figure (a)). RealMLP shows larger scale deviations and greater variation across members (Figure (b)), suggesting that these difficulties limit the gains of vanilla AdaQR on this backbone. This motivates an auxiliary regularizer for the scales inferred from the quantile spread and the smoothing output.

sections.heading: G.2 Auxiliary scale regularization
sections.text: We augment AdaQR with a regularizer that provides a direct training signal for the predicted scales. Following the notation of the proof in Appendix , let r = 1 − π ​ λ r=1-\sqrt{\pi}\lambda , with 0 < r < 1 0<r<1 . Under the assumptions of Proposition , the optimal scales satisfy σ t = 1 − r 2 ​ σ q = 1 − r 2 r ​ σ l . \sigma_{t}=\sqrt{1-r^{2}}\,\sigma_{q}=\frac{\sqrt{1-r^{2}}}{r}\,\sigma_{l}. This motivates two estimates of the noise standard deviation: s q = 1 − r 2 ​ σ ^ q , s σ = 1 − r 2 r ​ σ l , s_{q}=\sqrt{1-r^{2}}\,\widehat{\sigma}_{q},\qquad s_{\sigma}=\frac{\sqrt{1-r^{2}}}{r}\,\sigma_{l}, where, for N N predicted quantiles q j q_{j} at levels τ j \tau_{j} , we estimate the quantile-distribution scale as σ ^ q 2 = 1 N ​ ∑ j = 1 N ( q j − q ¯ ) 2 1 N ​ ∑ j = 1 N [ Φ − 1 ​ ( τ j ) ] 2 , q ¯ = 1 N ​ ∑ j = 1 N q j . \widehat{\sigma}_{q}^{2}=\frac{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}(q_{j}-\bar{q})^{2}}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}[\Phi^{-1}(\tau_{j})]^{2}},\qquad\bar{q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}q_{j}. Here, Φ \Phi is the standard normal CDF. The denominator accounts for the finite, symmetric quantile grid, recovering σ q 2 \sigma_{q}^{2} exactly for Gaussian quantiles. We supervise both estimates using CRPS evaluated at Gaussian CDFs F μ , s ​ ( z ) = Φ ⁡ ( z − μ s ) , μ = stopgrad ⁡ ( q ¯ ) , F_{\mu,s}(z)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{z-\mu}{s}\right),\qquad\mu=\operatorname{stopgrad}(\bar{q}), where stopgrad \operatorname{stopgrad} preserves its argument’s value but blocks gradients through it. The Gaussian CRPS has the closed form CRPS ​ ( F μ , s , y ) = e ⁡ ( 2 ​ Φ ​ ( e / s ) − 1 ) + 2 ​ s ​ ϕ ​ ( e / s ) − s π , e = y − μ , \text{CRPS}(F_{\mu,s},y)=e\bigl(2\Phi(e/s)-1\bigr)+2s\phi(e/s)-\frac{s}{\sqrt{\pi}},\qquad e=y-\mu, where ϕ \phi is the standard normal density. The resulting objective, denoted by AdaQR † , is ℒ AdaQR † = ℒ AdaQR + γ 2 ​ [ CRPS ​ ( F μ , s q , y ) + CRPS ​ ( F μ , s σ , y ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AdaQR}^{\dagger}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AdaQR}}+\frac{\gamma}{2}\left[\text{CRPS}(F_{\mu,s_{q}},y)+\text{CRPS}(F_{\mu,s_{\sigma}},y)\right], averaged over the training batch, with γ ≥ 0 \gamma\geq 0 controlling the regularization strength. Detaching q ¯ \bar{q} blocks the auxiliary gradient through the predicted mean, while centering the quantiles makes the spread estimate invariant to a common shift. The regularizer thus directly trains the quantile spread and the smoothing scale, although it can still affect point predictions through the shared backbone. Under the assumptions of Proposition , both inferred scales equal σ t \sigma_{t} at the population optimum. With the conditional mean correctly specified, s = σ t s=\sigma_{t} also minimizes the expected Gaussian CRPS. The auxiliary terms therefore share the same idealized scale optimum as AdaQR. The regularizer requires no architectural changes: we retain AdaQR’s scalar smoothing-scale output. At inference time, the point prediction remains the average of the predicted quantiles.

sections.heading: G.3 Effect on RealMLP
sections.text: As shown in Figure (b) and (c), AdaQR † produces noise-scale estimates that more closely match the true data uncertainty and are more consistent across ensemble members. The improvement primarily concerns the absolute scales, as vanilla AdaQR already ranks inputs by uncertainty reasonably well. These results suggest that the auxiliary regularizer helps RealMLP recover the scale relationship predicted by our theoretical analysis. sections.heading: Estimating data uncertainty.
sections.text: Following Kartashev et al. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.13909v1 [cs.LG] 09 Oct 2026 Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping https://github.com/dholzmueller/pytabkit Danil Rudenko Georgii Bulgakov Nikolay Kartashev Affiliation: Yandex Research, BRAInLab, HSE University Ivan Rubachev Affiliation: Yandex Research, BRAInLab, HSE University Daniil Krasylnikov Artem Babenko Affiliation: Yandex Research, BRAInLab, HSE University Abstract While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that uses input-dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at https://github.com/yandex-research/tabular-regression . 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Work done while at Yandex Research. 1. Introduction Despite the growing adoption of deep learning models for tabular data, in practice, it is not entirely clear what objective function should be used to solve regression tasks with DNNs. While the design of advanced regression objectives is an active research direction [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , the traditional Mean Squared Error (MSE) remains widely used. Existing studies evaluate alternative objectives on different datasets, backbones, and tuning protocols, making it difficult to establish which alternatives provide reliable improvements in practice. We revisit traditional and modern regression objectives on 41 established tabular datasets with extensive hyperparameter tuning, focusing on conventional DNNs (pretrained PFNs are outside our scope). We find that most objectives do not consistently improve over a carefully tuned MSE baseline. Two approaches stand out on MLP: Gaussian-smoothed binning objectives [ 1 , 2 ] , which represent targets as distributions over discrete bins, and quantile loss [ 9 ] , which predicts conditional quantiles of p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) via the pinball objective. Of these, quantile loss yields more consistent gains across different backbones. Related evidence comes from the PFN literature: TabICLv2 [ 10 ] adopts quantile loss for regression and reports benefits over MSE and binning; our findings complement this with a systematic comparison in conventional tabular models. Having identified quantile loss as a strong regression objective, we investigate a limitation that remains under standard training: regions with different levels of data uncertainty can reach their best predictive performance at different epochs. Consequently, a single early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions. Such input-dependent variation in target noise is common in tabular data [ 11 ] . We examine this conflict through controlled synthetic experiments and uncertainty-based checkpoint selection on real datasets. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Adaptive Quantile Regression (AdaQR), which incorporates jointly learned, input-dependent smoothing into quantile training. Effectively, by reducing the sensitivity of quantile updates to individual label realizations in high-uncertainty regions, adaptive smoothing aims to delay overfitting there while allowing learning to continue in lower-uncertainty regions. AdaQR is designed as one potential remedy for the mismatch induced by a shared stopping point, which improves upon standard quantile loss on several DNN backbones as we show in our experiments. Our main contributions are: • We benchmark 18 regression objectives on MLP across 41 datasets and evaluate selected objectives on three advanced tabular DNN backbones, using up to 100 hyperparameter tuning trials and the Muon optimizer [ 12 , 13 ] . • We show that most objectives do not consistently beat tuned MSE. Gaussian-smoothed binning objectives and quantile loss stand out on MLPs, while quantile loss provides more consistent gains across the tested backbones. • We identify a limitation of global early stopping in tabular regression: synthetic experiments reveal different preferred stopping epochs across noise levels, while real-data experiments show that selecting checkpoints separately for cohorts defined by estimated uncertainty can improve predictive performance over global selection. • We propose a new AdaQR objective that provides a jointly learned smoothing mechanism for investigating how uncertainty-aware training can mitigate stopping conflicts and evaluate this objective on established tabular backbones. 2. Related Work Regression objectives. Alternatives to MSE include robust losses [ 14 ] , target discretization [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , conditional distribution modeling [ 15 , 9 , 4 , 16 ] , and representation regularization [ 7 , 8 , 6 ] . We compare representative methods under a common tabular evaluation protocol and describe the individual objectives in the following sections. Early stopping and overfitting. Different parts of a model or subsets of the data can reach their best generalization performance at different training epochs. Heckel and Yilmaz [17] analyze different bias–variance tradeoffs across feature directions and network layers, showing that adjusting learning rates can improve early-stopping performance. Bao et al. [18] observe that some token groups are already overfitting while others remain underfit at the selected checkpoint in sequence-to-sequence models. Berta et al. [19] show that calibration and refinement errors are minimized at different stages of training, including in tabular classification. We extend the uncertainty-based analysis of tabular models [ 11 ] to training trajectories and checkpoint selection, examining how input-dependent noise relates to the epochs at which different regions achieve their best predictive performance. Heteroskedasticity-aware objectives and adaptive smoothing. A large body of work models input-dependent uncertainty in regression [ 20 , 21 ] . However, joint mean and variance estimation can introduce optimization difficulties [ 22 , 23 ] , motivating methods that preserve the mean-prediction accuracy of a corresponding MSE-trained model [ 24 ] . Related work on quantile regression investigates smoothing and local scale adaptation. Tan et al. [25] study convolution smoothing of the pinball loss to improve optimization and statistical estimation. Fasiolo et al. [26] derive covariate-dependent smoothing scales from a preliminary location–scale fit, while Jung et al. [27] estimate local scales using preliminary quantile or absolute-residual regressions. In distributional reinforcement learning, Malekzadeh et al. [28] propose a noise-motivated generalization of quantile-Huber loss with adaptive parameter adjustment. AdaQR combines an energy-distance objective with an input-dependent smoothing head learned jointly with the neural quantile predictor. We investigate this formulation through its effects on uncertainty-dependent training dynamics and tabular point prediction. 3. Revisiting regression objectives Notation. We consider supervised regression on tabular data. Let D = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 n D=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} denote a dataset, where x i ∈ ℝ d x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the feature vector and y i ∈ ℝ y_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is the target. We denote the neural model by f θ : ℝ d → ℝ d ′ f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}} , where the output dimension d ′ d^{\prime} depends on the objective and need not equal one. For pointwise objectives, the loss on an observation is l ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( x i ) , y i ) l(f_{\theta}(x_{i}),y_{i}) . 3.1 Losses Figure 1: Performance comparison of different objective functions using an MLP backbone across 41 BeyondArena datasets. ( Left ) Average rank performance across all datasets. ( Right ) Relative RMSE improvement over the standard MSE baseline, visualizing the magnitude of performance gains or degradation. The box plots visualize the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of the jitter plots. Notation details are provided in the beginning of Section . We compare the following regression objectives. Traditional losses. MSE penalizes squared errors, MAE penalizes absolute errors, and Huber loss [ 29 ] combines quadratic penalties for small errors with linear penalties for large ones. Binning-based losses. These methods discretize the target range into bins and train a categorical prediction head to match a target distribution. Hard Binning assigns each target to its nearest bin, while Soft Binning distributes probability mass according to Gaussian weights evaluated at bin centers [ 2 ] . HL-Gaussian instead integrates a truncated Gaussian density over each bin [ 1 ] . Joint end-to-end encoding learns the target distribution using an auxiliary encoder and a reconstruction objective [ 2 ] . All four methods return the predicted expectation over bin centers. Softmax-MSE uses the same prediction head but directly minimizes the squared error of this expectation [ 2 ] . Quantile regression. The model predicts a grid of conditional quantiles using the pinball loss [ 9 ] ; their average serves as the scalar prediction. Likelihood-based objectives. Gaussian NLL jointly learns a conditional mean and variance. β \beta -NLL reweights this objective by a detached power of the predicted variance to address optimization difficulties [ 22 ] . Mixture Density Networks model the conditional distribution as a Gaussian mixture [ 15 ] . The autoregressive approach of Song and Bahri [4] instead predicts tokenized targets using next-token cross-entropy. We evaluate both its normalized and unnormalized target encodings. Additional objectives and regularizers. GAR combines pointwise and pairwise terms to capture target values and their differences [ 5 ] . Ordinal Entropy [ 6 ] and ROT-REG [ 8 ] augment regression training with representation regularization, using entropy-based and optimal-transport-based terms, respectively. We provide a detailed description of all objectives in Appendix . 3.2 Experiments Datasets. We evaluate a subset of 41 regression datasets from BeyondArena [ 30 ] , excluding three computationally demanding datasets to keep hyperparameter tuning feasible within our 24-hour budget. Quantile regression under heteroskedasticity The benchmark in Section identifies several regression objectives that consistently outperform the MSE baseline. While HL-Gaussian and quantile regression (QR) perform comparably on a plain MLP, QR is more robust across backbones (Table ). Therefore, we focus on QR for the remainder of our analysis. QR predicts conditional quantiles without assuming a parametric family for p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) , allowing the predicted distribution’s shape and scale to vary across inputs. This flexibility is particularly beneficial for tabular data, where the conditional variance Var ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] \mathrm{Var}[y\mid x] , often termed data uncertainty , changes substantially with x x (i.e., the data is heteroskedastic ). Kartashev et al. [11] identify regions of low and high data uncertainty in several established tabular datasets, and demonstrate that dataset-wise aggregate scores often obscure how methods perform across these different regions. However, modeling input-dependent distributions does not guarantee that regions with different noise levels achieve their optimal predictive performance at the same epoch. Standard global early stopping selects a single checkpoint based on average validation error, applying it uniformly to all inputs. We first examine how prediction errors evolve during training across different uncertainty levels (Section ). We then test whether selecting checkpoints separately for different uncertainty cohorts improves upon doing so for random cohorts of the same size (Section ). Together, these experiments reveal an optimization challenge that distributional flexibility alone cannot resolve, motivating the adaptive objective introduced in Section . Both experiments in this section require a per-point estimate of data uncertainty and are most interpretable when this estimate is exact and test targets are noise-free. To demonstrate the claims of this section in a controlled environment that has these traits, we construct a synthetic dataset y = f ⁡ ( x ) + ε y=f(x)+\varepsilon , with noise added only to training targets, so test RMSE directly measures recovery of f = 𝔼 ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] f=\mathbb{E}[y\mid x] . We use two variants sharing exactly the same f f and x x : heteroskedastic , with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ ​ ( x ) 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma(x)^{2}) , and homoskedastic , with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) , serving as a control. Importantly, for this dataset, levels of true data uncertainty σ 2 \sigma^{2} are known to us exactly. See Appendix for details. To estimate uncertainty on real data we use a CatBoost model [ 35 ] trained via Gaussian negative log-likelihood on the real datasets, utilizing the predicted σ ⁡ ( x ) \sigma(x) as our uncertainty estimate. To prevent data leakage, this estimator is fit exclusively on the training split and applied to validation and test points during inference. 4.1 Optimal stopping epochs vary by uncertainty region In this subsection we investigate whether models require different stopping epochs for regions with varying data uncertainty. This requires analyzing the test error disaggregated by uncertainty level across epochs. The uncertainty plot [ 11 ] provides this perspective. Figure (a) shows an MLP trained with the quantile loss on the heteroskedastic synthetic dataset. Each curve corresponds to one epoch and displays the point-wise change in squared error relative to a reference epoch (the one with the best aggregate validation MSE), plotted against data uncertainty. Before the reference epoch, the model performs better on high-uncertainty points and worse on low-uncertainty ones; afterward, this trend reverses. In other words, the model starts overfitting high-uncertainty regions before it finishes fitting low-uncertainty ones, and the reference epoch is merely a compromise between these competing dynamics. To verify that this pattern stems from varying noise levels rather than intrinsic properties of x x or f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , Figure (c) repeats the experiment on the homoskedastic variant (same f f , constant noise scale, with samples sorted as in the heteroskedastic version). The effect disappears: performance changes across the displayed epochs are largely unrelated to the uncertainty ordering inherited from the heteroskedastic variant. Ideally, a model would retain its early-epoch error on high-uncertainty points while achieving its late-epoch error on low-uncertainty points, improving upon the QR baseline. However, Figure (a) only illustrates this misalignment on synthetic data and does not quantify the resulting performance loss. Section closes both gaps. Figure 2: In this synthetic experiment, heteroskedastic noise creates a mismatch between the stopping epochs preferred by low- and high-uncertainty regions, while AdaQR mitigates this effect. Uncertainty plots [ 11 ] for an MLP trained with (a) quantile loss and (b) AdaQR on the heteroskedastic dataset, and (c) quantile loss on the homoskedastic counterpart. Each curve shows the smoothed point-wise difference in squared test error relative to the reference epoch with the best aggregate validation MSE; negative values indicate improvement. Test samples are ordered by increasing uncertainty in the heteroskedastic dataset, with the same ordering used in all panels. Under heteroskedastic noise, earlier epochs perform relatively better on high-uncertainty points and later epochs on low-uncertainty points, indicating that different uncertainty regions favor different stopping times. This separation is reduced with AdaQR and disappears when the noise is homoskedastic. 4.2 Measuring the impact of epoch misalignment To quantify the performance penalty implied by the epoch misalignment in Figure (a), we evaluate a hypothetical strategy of per-cohort early stopping . This approach requires dividing the validation and test sets into groups of comparable data uncertainty, termed cohorts . To construct these, we compute the K − 1 K-1 empirical k K \tfrac{k}{K} -quantiles of the estimated uncertainty σ ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{\sigma}(x) on the validation set. These thresholds are used to split both the validation and test sets into K K cohorts, ordered from lowest (cohort 1 1 ) to highest (cohort K K ) uncertainty. Deriving these thresholds strictly from the validation set prevents data leakage, yielding equal-sized validation cohorts and test cohorts that are balanced up to sampling noise. With the cohorts established, we save a model checkpoint at every epoch during training. For each uncertainty cohort k k , we select the checkpoint e k ∗ e_{k}^{*} that minimizes the validation MSE restricted specifically to that group. During inference, each test point is routed to the checkpoint e k ∗ e_{k}^{*} corresponding to its uncertainty cohort. Because this approach assigns exactly one checkpoint to each test example, the resulting aggregated test RMSE reflects the empirical benefit of tailoring stopping times to local uncertainty levels. To accurately isolate this benefit, we cannot simply compare the resulting RMSE to standard global early stopping. While per-cohort selection allows the model to choose K K different epochs, each choice relies on only a fraction ( 1 / K 1/K ) of the validation data. To create a fair baseline, we apply the exact same procedure to random cohorts of matching size, created by randomly permuting the points before splitting. These random groups suffer the same penalty of smaller validation sets but contain no uncertainty information. Therefore, comparing uncertainty cohorts directly to random cohorts isolates the advantage of grouping by local noise levels. Table presents the relative improvements in test RMSE when using uncertainty-based (U) and random (R) cohorts compared to standard global (G) early stopping. To minimize the negative effects of smaller validation sets, we restrict this experiment to the seven largest datasets from our benchmark, reporting results for K = 5 K=5 and K = 10 K=10 . The results demonstrate that uncertainty-based selection improves median RMSE over global selection by 0.18% and 0.114% for five and ten cohorts, respectively. Under our comparison rule, both configurations record three wins, four ties, and no losses across the seven datasets. Furthermore, the drop in overall performance when increasing from K = 5 K=5 to K = 10 K=10 cohorts is consistent with increased checkpoint-selection noise from smaller validation subsets. The table also includes the homoskedastic variant of our synthetic dataset, which shares the same features x x and noiseless target function f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , but features a constant noise scale σ \sigma . This allows us to apply the exact same cohort splits used for the heteroskedastic variant. If σ ⁡ ( x ) \sigma(x) were merely acting as a proxy for partitioning the feature space into regions of similar inputs, both variants would show similar gains. Instead, performance on the homoskedastic version worsens when applying uncertainty-based splits, while the opposite is true for the heteroskedastic variant. Thus, the benefit stems specifically from adapting to how varying label noise alters training dynamics, not from the spatial structure of the inputs. Per-cohort early stopping, however, is not a practical solution: it requires storing numerous checkpoints and assigning test points to cohorts during inference. These results motivate adapting the objective to delay overfitting in high-uncertainty regions while allowing learning to continue in low-uncertainty regions. Adaptive quantile regression To address the stopping-time mismatch identified in Section , we introduce AdaQR, a quantile objective with jointly learned, input-dependent smoothing inspired by Adaptive Label Smoothing [ 36 ] . By applying stronger smoothing in high-uncertainty regions, we aim to postpone overfitting there. Up to quantile discretization, quantile loss is proportional to the squared Energy Distance between the predicted distribution and a Dirac δ \delta distribution at the observed target y y . Appendix details this connection through the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). To incorporate adaptive smoothing, we replace this point mass with a Gaussian distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( y , σ l 2 ) \mathcal{N}(y,\sigma_{l}^{2}) centered around the target, where σ l 2 \sigma_{l}^{2} is a learned variance predicted from the input x x . We design our loss function such that a larger conditional variance Var ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] \mathrm{Var}[y\mid x] yields a larger predicted σ l 2 \sigma_{l}^{2} . The first term is half of the squared Energy Distance, where the predicted distribution F F is estimated through the predicted quantiles q i q_{i} . The second term acts as a regularization penalty, scaling the predicted smoothing parameter σ l \sigma_{l} by a tunable hyperparameter λ \lambda . Conclusion In this paper, we systematically revisit regression objectives for tabular deep learning, comparing 18 objectives on 41 datasets and evaluating leading approaches across multiple backbones. Quantile loss emerges as a consistently strong alternative to carefully tuned MSE. Yet a strong objective does not eliminate the limitations of global early stopping: regions with different noise levels can peak at different training epochs, making a shared checkpoint a compromise. Motivated by this, we introduce AdaQR, which uses jointly learned, input-dependent smoothing as one possible remedy and improves predictions in several settings, with benefits varying across backbones and datasets. Our findings highlight that progress in tabular regression requires attention not only to what models optimize, but also to how different parts of the data are learned over time. 7. Limitations Our study identifies uncertainty-dependent stopping conflicts as an opportunity to improve tabular regression, but our understanding of the underlying training dynamics remains incomplete. AdaQR helps mitigate these stopping conflicts: on real datasets, cohort-based checkpoint selection yields smaller improvements for AdaQR than for standard quantile regression (Section ), yet still provides additional gains. This residual benefit suggests that adaptive smoothing does not fully resolve differences in preferred stopping times across uncertainty regions. Further work is needed to understand when these conflicts arise and to explore alternative objectives, training procedures, or checkpoint-selection strategies that can address them more effectively. AdaQR’s predictive gains also vary in magnitude across backbones, and its main evaluation excludes Tiny datasets, although results including them are reported in Appendix .
